member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.Igi2PresentationProvider
member.summary: Builds the renderers I.G.I. 2 draws with.

remarks.para: Only what exists. The sequel draws its placed world, its ground, its sky, its forests and water, and what its own player holds in front of its eyes (). Its title HUD draws weapon sights; the remaining HUD and map computer are pending. Every other factory is left at the interface's default of null, which the host reads as "this title does not present that pass" and skips.

Not here yet, and for one shared reason. The forest and the water are read and culled and tessellated, and neither is wired: both need the mission's model packs and its own archives, and a carries the level tree and the resource registry alone. That is a seam to widen deliberately once, with both passes in front of it, rather than twice by halves.

The world presenter itself is WorldRenderer, shared with Project I.G.I. It named no task type, no model id and no asset path, so it moved into the presentation layer and both titles draw through it; what differs is only how a level becomes placements, which is 's job.

The ground is registered for a rather than a , because the latter carries a TerrainSurface built from Project I.G.I.'s chunked octree and the sequel's flat grid of .thm tiles produces no such thing. Given the level and a registry, this reads its own.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.Igi2PresentationProvider.NightLuminance
member.summary: How dark a sun has to be before the picture is shown as night.

remarks.para: The band is fitted to what the sequel actually authors, which is the only thing available: the engine has no notion of exposure and nothing in a level says how bright to show it. Over the twenty-four levels the sun's luminance is either under 0.45 or over 0.55, with nothing in between — three night levels at 0.00, 0.11 and 0.15, a dusk one at 0.32, a dim mine at 0.41, and everything else from 0.56 to 0.99. So the band brackets a gap in the data rather than splitting a continuum, and every level lands firmly on one side of it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.Igi2PresentationProvider.NightBoundNightfall
member.summary: How dark a level has to read before the cycle binds it by its night end.
member.remarks: Three of the twenty-four are past this: location1/level1 at 0.85, location2/LEVEL6 at 0.94 and location3/LEVEL4 at 1.00, whose sun is literally black. The two below it are a dusk map at 0.24 and a dim one at 0.03, and both are far nearer a dim DAY than a night -- bound by their night end they would open at midnight, which is not what they are.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.Igi2PresentationProvider.NightReferenceHour
member.summary: The hour a night-bound level opens at: the darkest point of the cycle.

remarks.para: Midnight rather than an hour fitted per level, because the sequel gives no hour to fit one from -- every campaign level writes Time 12 and every multiplayer map writes Time 0, so the field is a constant and says nothing. Midnight is where the cycle's own handover is complete: the moon is fully risen and the sun fully faded, so the authored night is reproduced exactly rather than crossfaded with a sun on its way down.

Written as twenty-four rather than nought, which is the same instant: DayNightCycle.Apply reads a reference hour as > 0 and <= 24 -- nought is its "this level said nothing" -- and Reset wraps twenty-four back to nought for the clock itself. So this is midnight said in the one way both of them hear.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.ViewModel.Igi2ViewModelRenderer
member.summary: Draws what the player's view holds: the skinned first-person model and the models its clip hangs on it.

remarks.para: The view is a boned object drawn after the world under its own projection (HumanView_EnterHandler, igi2 0x4D5DB0, and vObjectFOV, tan 30°). Its model is skinned (arms1_1 in the first mission, a mesh of format 1), so its vertices are pushed through the posed bones whenever the pose moves, as the sequel's renderer weighs them (); the skin is built in the model's own frame and the model's position and orientation are applied in the draw.

The weapon in hand is not part of that model: each weapon's first-person clips carry an attach object named weapon on the right hand, and the engine draws the held weapon's Fixed Model there (WeaponMagicObj_GetModelName, 0x4733B0). The player says which model each part is; this resolves names to meshes and textures through the mission's pack table, as the placed world does.
None of the view's models has a bake, so each is lit as an unlightmapped object is: the level's fixed-function sun and object ambient per vertex (), the sun turned into the model's frame.
The same models drawn in the world are the weapons lying in the level (): rigid, unbaked, and lit the same way, under the world's projection.

member.summary: One of a water sheet's baked environment cube maps: six square faces, decoded and ready to become a cube texture.

remarks.para: What it holds, and what it hands over. The six faces as , in the order a cube sampler wants them, with the sampling rule written down — and , which turns them into a device cube map. When this type was first written the device had no cube entry point at all and this remark listed what one would need; three of the four items are now CreateCubeTexture, UpdateCubeFace and SetEnvironmentCube. The fourth, a draw path with three-component texture coordinates, is not needed after all: I.G.I. 2's water is drawn camera-relative, so a reflection direction can be built in the vertex stage out of the position and normal the mesh already carries.

Only water samples these. Envmap_LoadFromMemory has exactly one caller, Water_LoadEnvmapData (igi2ed 0x646810), and Envmap_Create (0x5817C0) has exactly one, the editor's water rebake. The *_DrawEnvmapHandler and *_EnumerateEnvmapHandler pairs on terrain, forests, the flat sky, rigid objects and spline objects point the other way: they are what gets drawn into a map while it is baked. Terrain_DrawEnvmapHandler (0x632E10) is a one-line forward to Terrain_EnterHandler, which settles it.

And only above quality zero. Water_LoadEnvmapData returns before reading anything unless WaterRender_GetQualityLevel() > 0, and WaterRender_Draw (0x577950) binds the cube to stage 0 in that case; at quality zero it binds the sheet's two ordinary 2D textures to stages 0 and 1 instead and the reflection is the flat Envmap image. So a port with no cube support is not rendering something wrong — it is rendering the original's low quality setting.

member.param: The surface point relative to the eye, in the engine's axes. Need not be normalized.

member.returns: The three-component direction to sample the cube with.

remarks.para: This is the whole of the original's rule, and it is readable rather than inferred: the water vertex shaders are not compiled into the binary, they are assembly source strings handed to D3DXAssembleShader at start-up by WaterRender_SetModeCallback (igi2ed 0x579740). The three of them live at 0x6B9B90, 0x6B98D0 and 0x6B95E8, and the third is the one that samples a cube:
remarks.code: dp3 r0.x, v0, v0 rsq r0.x, r0.x mul r0, r0.x, -v0 ; V = normalize(eye - surface) dp3 r2.x, r0, v1 ; V·N max r2.x, r2.x, c14.z ; clamped at vMaxReflectionAngle mul r3.x, r2.x, c5.w ; c5.w = 2.0 mad oT0.xyz, v1.xzy, r3.xxx, -r0.xzy ; (2(V·N)N - V).xzy
remarks.para: So the reflection is the ordinary one, and the swizzle is the whole answer to which face is which: the vector handed to the sampler is (R.x, R.z, R.y), the engine's Y and Z exchanged. That is what puts the engine's up axis on Direct3D's, and it is why the bake's third face — the camera looking along engine +Z, straight up — belongs in the POSITIVE_Y slot. The bake and the sampler were read from different functions and agree on all six.

The clamp is a parameter, not a constant. c14.z is loaded from WaterContext_t::vMaxReflectionAngle (offset 0x3C, set at 0x5789FB), the task's Max Reflection Angle (cos). Below that cosine the reflection stops opening out toward the horizon and stays where the cutoff puts it, which is why a grazing view of these sheets does not sample the sea floor. c5 is the literal vector (0, 0.5, 1, 2), set at 0x578957–0x57896C; that is where the 2 comes from.

The low-quality shader at 0x6B9B90 builds the same reflection and then does mul r1, r1, c11; add oT1, r1, c12 — a component-wise scale and offset, which cannot swizzle and cannot address a cube. That one is for the flat Envmap image on stage 1.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2ForestPresenter

remarks.para: The state is the original's, from igi2ed.exe. ForestRender_SetGenericState_Trunk (0x57C5A0) draws opaque with CULLMODE = CCW — the opposite winding to the terrain, which is CW — and with the fog density at DrawTerrainMesh_vFogDensity * 0.8, so a wood fogs a fifth less than the ground it stands on.

ForestRender_CreateBSPModel (0x57D160) scans a level's face groups for the first whose flags byte has bit 1 set and remembers its index; ForestRender_Draw (0x57CA90) then compares every group it draws against that index and sends the match through ForestRender_DrawFoliageFaceGroup and everything else through ForestRender_DrawTrunkFaceGroup. So the split is not a texture heuristic: it is a bit in the DNER record, at the byte this port's face-group reader treats as material properties.
The two are lit differently too, which is the corroboration: the trunk gets the grey average of the baked light's three bytes and the foliage gets the light itself under | 0xFF000000.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainPresenter
member.summary: Draws I.G.I. 2's ground: one additive pass per material, over the tiles a level declares.

remarks.para: The state this reproduces is the original's, read from igi2ed.exe rather than chosen: TerrainRender_SetBlendState (0x66BCB0) gives SRCBLEND = SRCALPHA with DESTBLEND = ONE, so the passes accumulate; TerrainRender_SetTextureState (0x66B810) modulates the material texture by the vertex diffuse and the detail texture onto that; and the vertex diffuse carries the baked terrain light in RGB with the material weight in alpha. and are the port's names for the same two things.

A vertex buffer per material, which is also the original's shape. A vertex's alpha is its weight for one material, so it cannot be shared between passes — and TerrainRender_AllocateMaterialVertexBuffers / ...UnlockMaterialVertexBuffers say the original reached the same conclusion. Each chunk therefore keeps only the vertices its own triangles touch, compacted, so the alpha is free to mean one material's weight.

Positions are stored relative to their tile's centre and drawn through , which folds the camera in at double precision. I.G.I. 2's coordinates reach millions of units, and the original solves the same problem the same way — TerrainRender_SetVertexShaderConstants builds its world matrix about the viewer.

Two modes, and the constructor chooses. Given
a level's detail controls it runs every frame and streams the result, which is what the original does — TerrainRender_Draw locks its vertex and index buffers at the top of the frame and refills them from the quadtree. Without them it uploads every tile at full detail once and draws all of it forever, which is correct and slow: 13,271,214 triangles across the corpus.
The full-detail path is kept rather than deleted because it is the reference the tessellated one is measured against — a quadtree that drops geometry is a bug that only shows as a comparison.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainPresenter.MaximumIndicesPerChunk
member.summary: The most indices one chunk holds before the next is started.
member.remarks:
The original's own budget. TerrainRender_DrawFace (igi2ed 0x66AAB0) keeps appending to a render chunk while its index count is <= 9997 and calls TerrainRender_AllocateRenderChunk when it is not, so a chunk holds at most 10,000 indices. Rounded down to a multiple of three here, which the original gets for free by appending three at a time.
It also settles a problem the device would otherwise have: indices are 16-bit, and a 512-sample tile drawn as one pass would want 262,144 vertices — four times what an index can name. Chunking at the original's budget keeps a chunk to 9,999 vertices at the very worst.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainPresenter.ChunkPoolSlots
member.summary: How many chunk pools take turns, one per frame.

remarks.para: A chunk cannot be rewritten while a frame in flight is still reading it. A storage mesh's buffers are host-visible and UploadMeshRange writes them directly, with no staging copy and no fence: the contract is that callers append, so the bytes a submitted frame reads are never touched again. The tessellated ground is the one caller that does not append — it refills the same chunks from offset zero every frame — so with two frames in flight the geometry the GPU was drawing was being overwritten underneath it, and triangles came out built from two frames' vertices at once: flat sheets and black wedges hanging off the ground, appearing only while the camera moved, because a still camera rewrites the same bytes.

One more than VulkanFrameLoop.MaxFramesInFlight, which is the same ring TerrainShadowCaster takes for the same reason: a pool written now was last submitted three frames ago, and those have retired. It costs two more copies of the chunks actually used — about half a megabyte each — rather than a stall.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2TextureLoader
member.summary: Turns an I.G.I. 2 texture name into a handle on the device, once per name.

remarks.para: Several materials share a texture — a level's ground is a handful of them over a great many tiles — so decoding and uploading each on demand, once, is the whole of this type.

A name is used exactly as written. A terrain material carries a full alias-qualified path with its own extension, MISSION:textures/k_grass.jpg, and that resolves through the file system to a loose file beside the level's archive. Only a bare name — which is how a model's materials name theirs — is expanded into LOCAL:textures/<name>.tex.

Three formats, because the game does not decode two of them itself. Direct3DTexture_DownloadFromFile (igi2ed 0x662FE0) hands the raw bytes to D3DXCreateTextureFromFileInMemoryEx, which sniffs and decodes whatever they are — so the sequel names .tex, .tga and .jpg interchangeably and the engine never notices. This sniffs the same way: a LOOP magic is the engine's own format, otherwise a TGA header shape, otherwise nothing.

All three are read here, so the ground, the sky and the props all texture. The sniffing order matters: LOOP and JPEG both have a magic number and TGA has none, so TGA is tried last and only its header shape can be checked.

A name the level does not ship resolves to rather than throwing. That is the original's own tolerance: a material whose texture is absent draws untextured, and the corpus has materials painted with textures their author later removed.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterPresenter
member.summary: Draws I.G.I. 2's water: a moving surface per sheet, reflecting the level's baked cube map.

remarks.para: The surface itself is exact. Every vertex is , which is Water_VertexFunction (igi2ed 0x645B30) read term for term: the sum of the sheet's wave trains, flattened with the vertex's depth in front of the eye, with the normal differenced from two neighbouring samples a hundredth of a wavelength away. The vertex the original builds is seven floats — a position, that normal, and how shallow the water is there — which is the same vertex this writes.
A sheet is a square. Water_IsUnderWater (0x6477D0) tests X and Y against Size independently rather than testing a distance, so what Size describes is a half-extent.

It is cut up again every frame, around the eye, by , which is WaterRender_Draw's subdivision. That matters for more than the shape: the water's light is computed at its vertices, so a sheet kilometres wide cut into an even grid shows every vertex as far away, and reads as a mirror to the bank.

It is drawn as the original's "High Water Quality". is WaterRender_azVertexShader[2] and its two texture stages: a Fresnel blend of the cube and the water's own light, the scene behind kept by how shallow the water is, and no surface texture at all.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterTessellation
member.summary: Cuts a sheet of water into triangles for one frame, finely near the eye and coarsely far from it: WaterRender_Draw's subdivision.

remarks.para: The sheet starts as its square's two triangles. Each triangle taken off the stack has its three edges measured: an edge is split when it is longer than the sheet's Detail times its distance from the eye (the nearest point on it), and never below half a metre. No edge split, the triangle is drawn; one, two or three, it is cut into two, three or four, which go back on the stack. A new vertex is a full sample of the surface (Water_VertexFunction) at the edge's middle, and then is drawn only part of the way from the edge's own midpoint towards it -- (length² / threshold − 1) × 0.3 of it, at most all -- so a vertex grows out of its edge as the eye closes on it rather than popping (WaterRender_CalculateRenderVertex). A triangle wholly off one side of the view is dropped.

The water's look is computed at the vertices, so this is what decides how the water looks, not just its shape: the reflection, the Fresnel term and the shallowness are all only as fine as these triangles are.
